trap: "Come to me" shrinks to a self-care slogan — Jesus as a place to relax — or the yoke gets reloaded into a heavier law where real Christians just try harder. Either way the strange logic is lost: that the road to rest runs through a yoke, and the door in is to become a child.
hinge: He promises rest and then hands you a yoke. A burden that is somehow light, a surrender that is somehow freedom. You cannot preach the comfort without the yoke, or the yoke without the comfort.

doors.claim: What looks like another demand is rest — the weary are not told to try harder but to trade the world's crushing yoke for a gentle one.

witnesses.author: Gregory the Great
witnesses.reading: It is a cruel yoke and a hard weight of servitude to be subject to the things of time, ambitious of earth, clinging to falling things — that is the burden Christ lifts.

witnesses.author: John Wesley
witnesses.reading: My yoke is easy — or rather gracious, sweet, benign, delightful; and my burden, contrary to those of men, is ease, liberty, and honour.

witnesses.author: Glossa ordinaria
witnesses.reading: How is the yoke of Christ sweet, when it is said: Narrow is the way that leadeth to life? It is narrow, because it is begun only with a narrow beginning, but in the course of time is widened with the unspeakable sweetness of love.

doors.say: You are carrying a yoke already; the only question is whose — come and trade it for the one that fits.
doors.do: Name one heavy thing they are dragging that Christ never asked them to carry, and have them lay it down this week.

doors.claim: The kingdom is not opened by being clever — it is hidden from the proud and shown to children, so the way in is down, not up.

witnesses.author: Augustine
witnesses.reading: The wise and understanding here are the proud; for who are the babes to whom it is revealed but the humble?

witnesses.author: Gregory the Great
witnesses.reading: He says not 'to the foolish' but 'to babes,' showing that he condemns pride, not understanding.

witnesses.author: John Wesley
witnesses.reading: Thou hast suffered these things to be hid from men, who are in other respects wise and prudent, while thou hast discovered them to those of the weakest understanding, to them who are only wise to Godward.

doors.say: You will not think your way into this; it opens to the ones small enough to receive it.
doors.do: Move the competent and capable in the room to one place they need to stop managing God and become a child again.

doors.landing: We piped and you did not dance
doors.claim: This generation rejects every tune — John's fast and Jesus' feast alike — always finding a reason to refuse God in whatever form God comes.

witnesses.author: Jerome
witnesses.reading: If fasting pleased you, why not John? If fulness, why not the Son of Man? One you called possessed, the other a glutton — no form of God would do.

witnesses.author: John Chrysostom
witnesses.reading: I and John came by opposite ways to do the same thing, like two hunters driving the same quarry from two sides — what excuse then is left?

doors.say: Notice how endlessly inventive we are at saying no to God — the austere prophet too grim, the joyful Lord too loose.
doors.do: Expose one excuse the hearer keeps ready for not answering God, and let it fall.

complementary.gravity: The day sets a humble king on a donkey (Zechariah), the Lord who is gracious and slow to anger (the Psalm), and Paul gasping "I do not do the good I want" (Romans 7) — and then Jesus: "Come to me, all you who are weary." The nerve: the gospel arrives not as one more demand on the competent but as rest for the worn-out and welcome for the unimpressive.

synthesis.convergence: Every reading sets strength against gentleness. The king comes not on a war-horse but a donkey (Zechariah); God is gracious and slow to anger (Psalm 145); Paul, worn out, cannot do the good he wills (Romans 7); and Jesus calls the weary to a yoke that is light. The day meets us at the end of our strength, not the height of it.
synthesis.claim: You do not have to be the strong one — the king is gentle, and his yoke is the one that finally carries you.
synthesis.here: For people who measure themselves by willpower and output — for whom Romans 7 is just Monday — the move is to stop white-knuckling the Christian life and come, weary, to the gentle king. Name where they are exhausted; hand them the donkey-riding Lord, not a heavier list.

doors.landing: Answered before the prayer was finished
doors.claim: The servant's prayer is answered while it is still unspoken: God has gone ahead of him to the well.

witnesses.author: John Wesley
witnesses.reading: Before I had done speaking in my heart — I spake it in my heart, so that none heard it but God, to whom thoughts are words, and from him the answer came.

doors.say: Before the servant finished praying, Rebekah was already walking toward the well. God was ahead of him.
doors.do: Ask them to name a prayer they have stopped praying because it seemed unheard, and to watch this week for what is already on its way.

doors.claim: When Rebekah finally sees Isaac she covers herself: the nearer the beloved comes, the more we feel our own unreadiness, and we are brought in anyway.

witnesses.author: John Wesley
witnesses.reading: She lighted off her camel, and took a vail and covered herself — in token of humility, modesty and subjection.

witnesses.author: Glossa ordinaria
witnesses.reading: Rebecca, having seen Isaac, learns who he is by asking the servant; and she straightway covered herself with a cloak, because the more she penetrates the mysteries of Christ, the more she is confounded at her past life.

doors.say: The closer she came to the one who loved her, the more she wanted to hide. He brought her into the tent anyway.
doors.do: Invite them to bring to God the part of their life they would rather veil, trusting they are wanted before they are ready.

semicontinuous.gravity: Abraham's servant finds his prayer answered before he has finished speaking it, and Rebekah says "I will go" to a husband she has never seen (Genesis 24); the Psalm bids a bride forget her father's house for a king who desires her; Paul cannot do the good he wants (Romans 7); and Jesus calls the weary to a yoke that is kind. The nerve: love comes looking for us, and asks for a yes before we can see where it leads.

synthesis.convergence: A servant travels far to find a bride and is answered before his prayer is out (Genesis 24); a bride is urged to leave her father's house for the king who desires her (Psalm 45); Paul finds he cannot do the good he wills (Romans 7); and Jesus invites the weary to learn from one gentle and lowly (Matthew 11). Each reading is a courtship: love goes out looking, and what it asks for is consent, not proven strength.
synthesis.claim: Rest is not earned but answered: God comes looking, and our whole part is Rebekah's — "I will go."
synthesis.here: For people worn down by trying harder, including the ones who know Paul's frustration from the inside, the move is to hear the invitation as courtship rather than assignment, and to answer it with consent rather than effort.

subtract: Three doors, three landings — rest for the weary, humility for the wise, the exposed excuse. Choose the one your people most need this week and let the other two go.
source: Catena Aurea (Aquinas; J.H. Newman tr., public domain), Wesley's Explanatory Notes, and the Glossa ordinaria (Migne recension, Wroot Press English), retrieved from ~/reception-corpus — attested, not authored.
